name: Adam
interpretive_note: Scripture presents Adam as a real historical individual through whom sin and death entered the human race (Romans 5:12-19) and as the counterpart to Christ, "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:22, 45). Evangelical scholars affirm Adam's historicity but are not unanimous on how the material details of Genesis 2 (formation from dust, a single first man as the sole biological ancestor of the whole human race) relate to the modern scientific account of human origins; young-earth, old-earth, and various "historical Adam" models all claim to uphold Adam's historicity while differing on how literally to read those details. This site follows the text's own presentation of Adam as a real, historical first man without adjudicating that underlying scientific debate.
source_summary: The first man, formed by God from the dust of the ground and placed in the Garden of Eden; his disobedience in eating the forbidden fruit brought sin and death into the world, and Paul contrasts him with Christ, the "last Adam," whose obedience reverses what Adam's disobedience began.
family_friendly_summary: God made the very first man, Adam, by shaping him from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him. God placed Adam in a beautiful garden called Eden and gave him one simple rule: don't eat fruit from one particular tree. God made Eve to be Adam's wife and companion, and the two cared for the garden together. But a sneaky serpent tricked Eve into eating the forbidden fruit, and Adam ate it too, even though he knew better. This first act of disobedience -- often called "the Fall" -- brought trouble, hard work, and death into the world, and Adam and Eve had to leave the garden. Even so, God didn't abandon them: He made clothes for them and stayed with them. The Bible later calls Jesus the "last Adam," because Jesus came to undo, through His perfect obedience, the harm that Adam's disobedience caused.
adult_story: Adam is formed by God "from the dust of the ground" and given life by God's own breath (Genesis 2:7), placed in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it (2:15). When none of the animals proves a fitting companion, God causes a deep sleep to fall on Adam and builds Eve from his rib; Adam's exclamation over her ("bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh") is Scripture's first recorded human speech (2:18-24). God's one command -- not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil -- is the boundary Adam is given, and he breaks it: present with Eve when the serpent tempts her, Adam eats the fruit she gives him without recorded protest (3:6), and Romans 5:12-14 lays responsibility for sin entering the world at Adam's feet specifically, even though Eve ate first. Confronted by God, Adam's answer -- blaming both Eve and, implicitly, God himself ("the woman whom You gave to be with me") -- is the first recorded act of human self-justification. Consequences follow: cursed ground, painful labor, death, and exile from Eden (3:17-19, 23-24). Yet even in judgment God clothes Adam and Eve (3:21) and later grants them Seth after Cain kills Abel (4:25). Paul names Adam as the historical head under whom all humanity is bound to sin and death, and, by contrast, as the type of Christ, "the last Adam," whose obedience reverses what Adam's disobedience began (Romans 5:12-19; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45).
christ_connections: Paul names Adam directly as the historical counterpart to Christ, "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45) -- where Adam's disobedience brought sin and death to all who are in him, Christ's obedience brings righteousness and life to all who are in Him (Romans 5:18-19).

Adam's instinctive self-justification when confronted with his sin -- blaming Eve, and implicitly God -- is the pattern Christ's obedience reverses: where Adam fled responsibility, Christ embraced it fully on behalf of others.

God's act of clothing Adam and Eve after their sin, at the cost of an animal's life, is Scripture's first picture of atonement covering shame -- anticipating the greater covering Christ's own sacrifice provides.
